terms.meaning: A part of an ocean reaching far inland, smaller than an ocean, such as the Arabian Sea.
A part of an ocean or sea that cuts into the land, smaller than a sea, such as the Gulf of Mannar.
A small half-circle of water partly surrounded by land, such as the Bay of Bengal.
A narrow strip of water joining two large water bodies, such as the Palk Strait.
A narrow strip of land joining two large land masses; a place for ocean canals.
The amount of salt dissolved in sea water, in parts per thousand (ppt).
The regular rise and fall of the sea level.

items.name: Canals across isthmuses
items.formula: Suez: between Asia and Africa. Panama: between North and South America.
items.example: Both cut through a narrow neck of land.

items.name: Continental shelf
items.formula: The shallow area by the coast, about 100 fathoms deep on average (1 fathom = 6 ft).
items.example: 100 fathoms = 600 ft. Good for fishing and minerals.

items.name: Continental slope and deep sea plain
items.formula: Slope: steep, with submarine canyons. Plain (abyssal plain): the largest area, with sea mounts and guyots.
items.example: The slope links the shelf and the plain.

items.name: Deepest point of the oceans
items.formula: Challenger Deep of the Mariana Trench, about 10,929 metres, in the Pacific.

items.name: Ocean temperature
items.formula: Warmer near the equator and colder with depth.
items.example: Sunlight reaches only about 200 metres down.

items.name: Average salinity
items.formula: 35 ppt, which is 35 grams of salt in 1000 grams of water.
items.example: Highest near the tropics and lowest near the poles.

items.name: Why the sea is salty
items.formula: Rivers bring salts; the water evaporates and the salt stays.
items.example: Over a long time salt builds up.

items.name: Very salty water bodies
items.formula: Lake Van (Turkey), the Dead Sea, Lake Sambar (India) and the Red Sea.
items.example: Lake Van is the saltiest of these.

items.name: Warm and cold currents
items.formula: Warm: from the equator towards the poles. Cold: from the poles towards the equator.
items.example: Earth's rotation, temperature, wind and salinity drive them.

items.name: Pacific Ocean currents
items.formula: Warm: Kuroshio, East Australian. Cold: Oyashio, California, Peru (Humboldt).
items.example: The West wind drift is also cold.

items.name: Atlantic Ocean currents
items.formula: Warm: Gulf Stream, North Atlantic drift, Brazilian. Cold: Labrador, Canary, Falkland, Benguela.
items.example: The Norwegian current is cold too.

items.name: Indian Ocean currents
items.formula: North: change direction with the monsoon. South: warm Mozambique, Madagascar, Agulhas; cold West Australian.
items.example: So the north Indian Ocean has seasonal currents.

items.name: Major fishing grounds
items.formula: Where warm and cold currents meet: Kuroshio and Oyashio off Japan; Gulf Stream and Labrador at the Grand Bank.
items.example: The Dogger Bank is in the North Sea.

items.name: Timing of tides
items.formula: High to low tide: 6 hrs 13 minutes. High to high: 12 hrs 26 minutes.
items.example: In 24 hrs 52 minutes there are 2 high and 2 low tides.

items.name: Spring and neap tides
items.formula: Spring: Sun, Moon and Earth in a line (new and full moon), highest highs. Neap: Moon at a right angle (quarter days), weaker tides.
items.example: Tides come from the pull of the Moon and Sun.

items.name: Uses of tides
items.formula: Navigation, keeping harbours clean, salt making, fishing and tidal energy.
items.example: They also help in choosing port sites.

mistakes.text: A strait is water joining two seas; an isthmus is land joining two land masses.
Spring tides have nothing to do with the spring season: they happen at new moon and full moon.
Warm currents flow away from the equator; cold currents flow towards it.
